title: Trump Criticizes Supreme Court Justices and Signs a New 10% Tariff Order
description_medium: After the Supreme Court struck down his use of emergency powers for tariffs, Donald Trump called the justices who opposed him “fools” and said he would continue the policy through other legal authorities. Later on February 20, 2026, he signed an order imposing a new 10% tariff under a 1974 trade law. The law limited the duties to 150 days unless Congress extended them. The new order followed, but did not reverse, the Court’s ruling.
description_long:
On February 20, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled against Donald Trump’s use of emergency powers to impose international tariffs. Trump responded at a White House appearance by calling the justices who had rejected the policy “fools” and “lapdogs,” and said he would pursue the same trade agenda under another legal authority. He also accused the Court of being influenced by foreign interests without providing evidence for that claim. Later that day, he signed an executive order imposing a new 10% global tariff under a 1974 law. The Los Angeles Times reported that the statute limited the tariffs to 150 days; extending them would require congressional approval. The order was a new action taken after the Court’s decision, not a continuation under the authority the Court had rejected.

The ruling and the response left different questions open: it constrained Trump’s reliance on emergency powers, while the administration moved to another statutory route. The article discussed other possible trade authorities as well, but those were options under consideration, not all actions completed that day. The reporting documents both Trump’s criticism of the justices and his signed replacement order.
evidence_notes: LA Times reports 6–3 ruling, Trump’s reaction, signed EO later that day, 10% levy under 1974 statute and 150-day statutory limit absent congressional extension. Distinguish this signed order from other possible trade-law routes discussed.
corrected_wording: Retained the event title while replacing generic catalog text and clarifying what Trump signed versus alternative authorities merely discussed.

title: DHS Spokesperson Tricia McLaughlin to Leave During Scrutiny of ICE Raids
description_medium: The Department of Homeland Security confirmed that spokesperson Tricia McLaughlin would leave the agency in the week after February 17, 2026. She had been one of the administration’s most visible defenders of deportation raids and had publicly defended federal officers after the fatal shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis. DHS said she had planned to leave in December but stayed after the shootings. Her departure came as the agency faced heightened scrutiny and House Democrats filed impeachment articles against Secretary Kristi Noem.
description_long:
DHS confirmed on February 17, 2026, that Tricia McLaughlin, its top spokesperson, would leave the department the following week. The Guardian described her as one of the most prominent public defenders of the Trump administration’s deportation raids. After Renee Good was killed by federal immigration officers in Minneapolis, McLaughlin said in a DHS statement that citizens as well as noncitizens were attacking law enforcement. After Alex Pretti was shot, she told the Guardian that he had “violently resisted” and that officers had fired defensive shots. The Guardian reported that DHS said McLaughlin had originally planned to leave in December but stayed because of the shootings.

Her announced departure coincided with intense scrutiny of the department’s immigration enforcement, including public backlash after the Minneapolis killings. House Democrats had filed articles of impeachment against Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, citing the deaths and alleging failures of public trust and congressional oversight. The report does not say McLaughlin’s departure was a firing or that it resulted from a formal investigation. It records a planned personnel change during a period when DHS’s public account of enforcement operations was under strong challenge.
evidence_notes: Guardian attributes the December departure plan and decision to stay to DHS; it identifies her statements about Good and Pretti and the broader scrutiny. It does not report a firing or state that backlash caused her departure.
corrected_wording: Removed generic editorial impact language; described the announced departure, prior public statements, and contemporaneous scrutiny with attribution.

title: Washington Coal Club Honors Trump as He Orders Pentagon Coal Power Contracts
description_medium: At a White House ceremony on February 11, 2026, Washington Coal Club representatives presented Donald Trump with a trophy naming him the “undisputed champion of beautiful clean coal.” The event coincided with his executive order directing the Defense Department to seek long-term power-purchase agreements with U.S. coal plants for military and other critical facilities. The Department of Energy separately announced $175 million for upgrades at six coal-fired plants. The order directs procurement efforts; it does not itself specify completed contracts.
description_long:
Donald Trump received a coal-themed trophy at a White House ceremony on February 11, 2026, the day he signed an executive order directing the Defense Department to seek long-term power-purchase agreements with coal-fired plants serving military installations and other mission-critical facilities. The Guardian reported that the award was granted by the Washington Coal Club, an advocacy organization with financial ties to the coal industry, and that Peabody Energy chief executive James Grech presented it. Coal executives, miners and administration officials attended. The order frames coal generation as important to national defense and instructs the department to prioritize reliability, fuel security and mission assurance when seeking agreements. It directs the pursuit of contracts; it does not itself identify signed deals or a total purchasing commitment.

At the same event, Trump said the military would buy more coal power. The Energy Department announced a separate $175 million in funding for six projects to modernize or extend coal plants in West Virginia, Ohio, North Carolina and Kentucky. That grant program was presented as part of a broader $525 million effort. The award, procurement direction and plant-modernization grants were related elements of the administration’s coal policy but distinct actions with different funding and implementation mechanisms.
evidence_notes: Guardian identifies Washington Coal Club, the award and ceremony; White House EO text says the Defense Department shall seek long-term PPAs, not that contracts were completed. DOE confirms a separate $175m program for six projects. Distinguish amount and implementation.
corrected_wording: Replaced source-gap caveats with facts from the linked Guardian report and primary White House and DOE announcements; explicitly separates proposed procurement from completed contracts.

title: Tom Homan Said Targeting Deportations Could Preserve Public Support
description_medium: In a June 2025 interview with NBC’s Julia Ainsley, border czar Tom Homan argued that prioritizing immigrants convicted of crimes would help retain public support for deportations. The Guardian reported the remarks as the Trump administration’s broad enforcement operations faced scrutiny after fatal shootings by immigration officers in Minneapolis. It also cited arrest figures showing that fewer than 14% of nearly 400,000 people arrested by ICE in the first year of Trump’s second term had charges or convictions for violent crimes.
description_long:
Tom Homan, the Trump administration’s border czar, said in a June 2025 interview with NBC correspondent Julia Ainsley that deportation policy should prioritize people convicted of crimes. The Guardian reported the remarks in February 2026, after Homan had been sent to Minnesota following the fatal shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal immigration officers. Homan said that concentrating on criminal cases would help maintain public confidence and that enforcement should be carried out humanely. The interview was conducted for Ainsley’s forthcoming book on mass-deportation policy, rather than as a new directive issued during the Minnesota deployment.

The Guardian contrasted Homan’s stated prioritization with federal enforcement figures reported by CBS: among nearly 400,000 immigrants arrested by ICE during the first year of Trump’s second presidency, fewer than 14% had charges or convictions for violent criminal offenses. That figure measures violent-crime records, not all criminal charges or immigration violations. The article also described the broad and sometimes violent enforcement operations, protests in several cities and the Minneapolis deaths. Homan’s remarks set out a public rationale for prioritization; they do not demonstrate that ICE operations consistently followed it or that a formal policy changed after the interview.
evidence_notes: Guardian dates the interview to June 2025 and links the comments to Ainsley’s book. It reports the under-14% figure as people arrested in Trump’s first second-term year with violent-crime charges/convictions. Do not conflate that with all criminal histories or describe remarks as a new policy directive.
corrected_wording: Added the original interview timing and framed Homan’s comments as stated strategy, not proof of actual enforcement practice; replaced generic consequences with the specific comparison in the report.

title: Ruben Gallego Proposes National Strike if Trump Interferes in Midterms
description_medium: Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego proposed a general strike if the Trump administration tried to interfere with the 2026 midterm elections. He named scenarios such as stopping ballot counts, seizing ballots or surrounding polling places. Gallego was responding to Trump’s call for Republicans to “take over” and “nationalise” voting in unspecified locations. The Guardian reported the proposal as conditional; the article did not report that election interference or a national strike had occurred.
description_long:
On February 5, 2026, Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego said Americans should consider a nationwide strike if the Trump administration tried to disrupt the November midterm elections. In an interview on the Court of History podcast, he described possible worst-case scenarios: officials seizing ballots during counting, stopping a count or surrounding polling places. Gallego urged workers across sectors to stay home if such interference occurred. His remarks followed President Donald Trump’s call for Republicans to “take over” voting in at least 15 locations, which Trump did not identify, alongside repeated false claims of widespread election fraud. The Guardian also reported that the Justice Department was suing states over voter rolls and that the FBI had searched an election office in Georgia’s Fulton County for 2020 election records.

Gallego’s proposal was a warning about a possible future response, not a report that Trump or federal officials had carried out the hypothetical actions. The article described it against a broader dispute over federal involvement in election administration, including Trump’s public comments about nationalizing elections and White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt’s statement that she had heard no formal plan to station ICE near polling places. The account documents the senator’s conditional call for mass protest and the political circumstances surrounding it; no strike had begun.
evidence_notes: Guardian reports the conditional scenarios, podcast setting, Trump’s nationalization remarks, voter-roll suits, Georgia search and White House response. Keep Gallego’s proposed strike separate from completed events.
corrected_wording: Removed generic impact language and preserved the conditional nature of the senator’s proposal and the separate status of the reported election-related actions.
